# **Discrete-Survival Compatibility Score for Donor-Recipient** **Matching in Liver Transplantation**
Yingke Wang [†,*], Eunice Tan [‡], Yingji Sun [‡], Mamatha Bhat [‡], Xi He [†,] _[⋄]_, Sirisha Rambhatla [†, **] - University of Waterloo - University Health Network _⋄_ Vector Institute

**Abstract** Liver transplantation is a life-saving treatment for patients with end-stage liver disease. However, donor organ scarcity and patient heterogeneity make optimal donor recipient matching a persistent challenge. In this work, we present a two-step approach that models post-transplant survival probabilities at clinically relevant discrete time points and combines the predictions into a compatibility score for each donor-recipient pair. Our findings suggest that, for the multi-center liver transplant dataset, our approach yields higher accuracy than directly estimating a single compatibility score. By integrating statistical and machine learning techniques into a cohesive framework, empirical results show that our method outperforms traditional methods while preserving clinical interpretability, which enables more nuanced donor-recipient matching and supports practical decision-making in real-world clinical settings. **Keywords:** Machine Learning, Healthcare, Evidence-Based Medicine, Interpretability.

chunks.raw_text: [1]. However, the allocation of donor livers is complicated by the persistent problem of organ shortage, where the demand for transplants far exceeds the supply [2]. This scarcity pressures clinicians to ensure that each graft offers the maximum possible survival benefit. One of the most straightforward approaches is to develop a post-transplant risk score or, equivalently, a donor-recipient compatibility score. Clinicians sometimes use established liver transplant risk scores, including the DMELD score [3], Balance of Risk (BAR) score [4], and other specialized indices [5, 6]. While these tools provide valuable heuristics, they often fail to capture the full complexity of donor-recipient matching and do not consistently yield optimal outcomes, nor are they used by transplant centers [7]. Alongside established clinical scores, recent advances in machine learning (ML) and deep learning have produced several survival models (e.g., DeepSurv [8]) that can estimate hazard or survival time, helping determine whether a donor-recipient pair is an optimal match. Yet, although these models are researched in several clinical papers [9, 10], these approaches are not fully integrated into clinical practice, due to poor generalizability and performance on large, heterogeneous clinical cohorts [11]. Moreover, as individual transplant center records data differently, aggregating the data together into a multi-center scale results in a high-dimensional and high-missingness dataset, degrading ML models’ predicting power, suggesting ML models only work for the local dataset [12]. However, it is crucial to establish a universal framework that can advise clinicians on liver donor and candidate compatibility at a multi-center scale to maximize organ utility. Therefore, our research problem is to develop a system that broadly assesses donor–recipient compatibility and effectively distinguishes between short and long

chunks.raw_text: (1) **Two-Step Compatibility Score.** We propose _DisCScore_, which avoids direct survival-risk estimation by first predicting binary (death/survival) outcomes at discrete time points, then aggregating them into a single compatibility score. This method excels on heterogeneous clinical data where extensive missingness and numerous categorical variables are present. (2) **Interpretability.** _DisCScore_ employs clinically meaningful features closely aligned with those used by experts in donor–recipient matching decisions. This alignment makes its predictions more transparent to practitioners, facilitating easier validation and adoption in clinical workflows. (3) **Performance.** _DisCScore_ consistently outperforms both established clinical scores and contemporary ML models in distinguishing between short- and long-term donor recipient survival through extensive experiments. Particularly for recipients who experience early post-transplant mortality versus those who surpass early critical thresholds, our model demonstrates a 3% improvement in accuracy compared to the best existing baseline.

chunks.raw_text: **Survival Models** . We can estimate how compatible the liver and the recipient are by using survival models. Traditional regression approaches fail to handle these outcome variables properly as, in our case, not all patients reach graft failure by the end of the study. Hence, a dedicated survival analysis framework is essential [14]. Over the past several decades, various methods have been employed, ranging from classical survival models to more sophisticated machine learning and deep learning techniques. Beginning with the Cox Proportional Hazards (CoxPH) mode [15], it is one of the first methods that produce individualized survival prediction over time. It offers interpretable coefficients on features but often struggles with complex donor-recipient interactions with non-linear extension. Moving forward, we have neural network-based survival models like DeepSurv [8] and DeepHit [16]. DeepSurv adapts the CoxPH framework by replacing the linear predictor with a neural network that learns a non-linear representation of covariates [17]. While DeepSurv builds upon the Cox model’s risk-based approach, DeepHit employs a deep neural network to learn a discretized representation of the survival function at a list of time points. However, deep neural networks are prone to overfitting, particularly if data quality is insufficient, prevalent in heterogeneous clinical datasets [18, 19]. Unlike previous methods, tree-based survival approaches, such as Random Survival Forest (RSF) [20], are particularly well-suited to heterogeneous clinical datasets that often contain substantial missing data due to inconsistent recording styles across health organizations

Because tree-based models can inherently handle missing values by treating them as a separate category during node splitting [21], they simplify the data preparation process by eliminating the need for explicit imputation. In addition, they capture non-linear and interaction effects among donor and recipient attributes without requiring explicit transformations, making them well-suited to the high-dimensional, heterogeneous data commonly encountered in medical registries [22]. It also offers interpretability measures such as variable importance, enables investigators to identify survival’s main drivers, and provides explanatory insights to clinicians [20]. **Survival Models in Liver Transplantation** . The application of machine learning to predict compatibility or predict outcomes in liver transplantation and optimal donor has been researched as the rise of Artificial Intelligence [18, 23, 24]. Recently, Börner et al. [23] has demonstrated that using discrete time points to model post-transplant outcomes is promising on a homogeneous liver transplant dataset. However, the performance of applying ML techniques to heterogeneous transplant data is unsatisfactory. Briceño et al. [11] investigated neural network performance on the United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS) database, including patient-level data across all transplant centers in the United States. The authors noted that the UNOS dataset contains a significant amount of incomplete data, with only 28 variables having less than 10% missing data, resulting in poor data learning performance.

chunks.raw_text: **Clinical Scoring in Liver Transplantation** . In parallel with ML approaches, numerous clinical scoring systems have been developed to assist in liver allocation and post-transplant prognostication. The Donor Risk Index (DRI) [25] is one early example that summarizes donor quality into a single metric. D-MELD score [3], improves graft compatibility of traditional MELD score by considering donor age. The Survival Benefit model [6] attempts to quantify the net survival gain from transplantation compared to remaining on the waitlist, while the Balance of Risk (BAR) score [4] integrates donor and recipient factors to reflect clinical reality better. Although these scoring systems are easy to implement and interpret, their static nature and limited feature sets often fail to capture complex, time-varying interactions [26].

chunks.raw_text: **Challenge with Single Step Prediction.** A direct estimation of the compatibility score seems natural to implement and convenient for numerical comparison. However, as mentioned in Section 2, natively applying neither the survival models nor clinical scores to predict a single risk score would not yield promising outcomes in aggregated multi-center transplant datasets. Instead, we will predict survival probabilities at a series of discrete time points. By modeling each time point as a separate label, the model can learn a probability that captures how likely the event will occur within each interval. This multi-label scheme is generally more straightforward to estimate because it focuses on the likelihood of surviving past critical milestones rather than pinpointing the exact event time, which has been shown to yield higher accuracy and precision in prior research [27].

chunks.raw_text: In this section, we detail the technical framework of our approach to donor-recipient matching in Figure 1. We selected multi-label XGBoost [13] as our prediction model and adapted it to survival analysis to consider censored individuals. We name our model _Disc-_ _SurvBoost_ to emphasize it predicts discrete binary survivals. In addition to the benefit of the tree-based model mentioned in Section 2, XGBoost combines tree structure with gradient boosting, building each tree to correct the errors of the previous ones. This iterative improvement often yields more accurate models than bagging methods (like Random Forest), where all trees are trained independently. After detailing our prediction model on discrete time points, we then describe the construction of the score capable of identifying the most compatible donor for any given transplant recipient based on the model’s prediction on each discrete time point.

chunks.raw_text: The following introduces the necessary evaluation metrics for our subsequent validation. Both metrics determine how well our method performs in discriminative ability. One focuses on discriminative ability over the entire period, while the other focuses on discriminative ability at a specific time. **C-index (Harrell’s Concordance Index).** In survival analysis, Harrell’s Concordance Index (C-index) [29] is a widely used metric for evaluating a model’s discriminative ability. Values of C-index near 0.5 indicate that the score predictions are no better than a coin flip in determining which patient will live longer. Values near 1 indicate that the scores are good at determining which of two patients will have the disease first. **Time-Dependent ROC and AUC** . At a specific time _t_, the time-dependent ROC curve compares individuals who fail by _t_ with those who survive beyond _t_, thereby measuring model discrimination at _t_ . The corresponding area under this curve, AUC( _t_ ), quantifies the probability that the model assigns a higher risk score (lower compatibility score) to the individual who fails earlier [30]. Similar to the classical ROC, an AUC( _t_ ) of 0.5 indicates random guessing at time _t_, whereas a value near 1.0 signifies strong discriminative ability.

chunks.raw_text: **Interprebility.** Due to the inherent transparency and interpretability of XGBoost, we present the top 20 most frequently selected features in the _DiscSurvBoost_ in Fig 3 and their description in Appendix B. These features align closely with the clinical variables that practitioners regularly consider in transplant decision-making. As a result, the model’s outputs are not only empirically robust but also clinically credible, strengthening its utility in real-world medical contexts. **C-index.** To assess the overall discriminatory power of our compatibility score, we calculated Harrell’s C-statistic [29] for the entire study period (2009 to 2019), shown in Table 1. Our _DiscSurvBoost_ model demonstrated a strong ability to differentiate between shorter and longer donor-recipient pair survival times, achieving a C-index of 0.8601 with a 95% confidence interval (CI) of [0 _._ 859 _,_ 0 _._ 861]. This performance surpassed that of the best-performing baseline model, DeepHit, which had a C-index of 0.8502. Noticing the clinical scores, DMLD and BAR are at a much lower precision level due to their simple expression. **Timed-ROC and Timed-AUC.** To evaluate and compare the predictive performance of the survival models at specific time points, we drew the time-dependent Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (ROC) and calculated the area under (AUC) of _DisCScore_ and other survival models (Coxph, DeepSurv, _RSF_, etc.) at half-year, 1-year, and 3-years posttransplant periods. Employing multiple time points from short and middle-range follow-up periods, it provides a comprehensive evaluation of our method in an early stage, the high-risk period for liver graft failure. The time-ROC results in Figure 4 show that _DisCScore_ (the blue line) always sits on top of other benchmarks, demonstrating its superior discriminative power at these time points.
